title: Boats to Save People
summary: You get a list `people` of body weights and an integer `limit`, and you have as many boats as you need. A boat carries one person, or a pair of people whose weights add up to at most `limit`. No one weighs more than `limit`. Return the fewest boats that carry everyone.

examples.explanation: The 5 can't share with anyone (even 1 + 5 = 6 is over 5), so it goes alone; then 1 + 4 and 2 + 3 share boats.
Pair 1 with 5 and 2 with 3. Putting the two lightest together (1 + 2) would leave 3 and 5, who can't share (8 > 6), so that takes 3 boats.

constraints: people is in no particular order

approaches.twist: Sort, then put the heaviest person in each boat and add the lightest one whenever the two fit.
Scan the rest for each person's heaviest partner who still fits, and pair them.
approaches.note: Works, but scanning everyone for each person takes O(n²) time, about 2.5·10⁹ checks for 5·10⁴ people, plus O(n) space to mark who has a seat. The target is O(n log n) time and O(1) space.

signals.meaning: A boat holds at most two, so the answer is a pairing. After sorting, the heaviest person's best partner is the lightest one: if even the lightest doesn't fit, no one does, and the heaviest rides alone.
Fill the boats greedily: each one takes the heaviest person left, plus the lightest when the two fit. Pairing the two extremes never costs an extra boat.
Sort first so the lightest and heaviest people sit at the two ends. O(n log n) for 5·10⁴ people is fast.

constraintReading: len(people) can reach 5·10⁴, so scanning for a partner for every person (O(n²), about 2.5·10⁹ checks) is too slow. Sorting costs O(n log n), and then one inward pass seats everyone in O(n). Sorting in place keeps the extra space O(1).

related.relation: Same inward pointers on sorted numbers, but they hunt for an exact sum instead of checking whether two weights fit under a limit.
